title: Abu Bakr's words
hookLine: Abu Bakr says whoever worshiped Muhammad, he has died, and whoever worships Allah, He lives (3:144)
carry: allah is alive and does not die

cards: When someone at the center of everything dies, the first hours are chaos. People don't believe it. Someone insists the doctors are wrong.
Someone else can't stop crying. That was Medina that Monday. News spread from Aisha's room into the mosque and out into the streets.

And 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, the strongest-willed man among the companions, stood up in the mosque and refused to accept it. The Prophet ﷺ hasn't died, he said; he'll come back. The crowd was coming apart.
Then Abu Bakr rode in from his house at the edge of town.

teach.b: Sahih al-Bukhari tells it step by step. Abu Bakr spoke to no one first. He went straight into Aisha's room, where the Prophet lay covered with a cloth.

He uncovered his face, bent down and kissed him, and wept, and said: you were good in life, and you are good in death. Then he walked out into the mosque, where 'Umar was still talking, and told him to sit down.
And he spoke to the crowd, one of the most remembered sentences in Muslim history: whoever worshiped Muhammad, Muhammad has died. And whoever worships God, God is alive and does not die.
Then he recited a verse from the third surah.
In Pickthall's translation it begins: "Muhammad is but a messenger," goes on to say that messengers had passed away before him, and asks: if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?

They all knew that verse. It had come down years earlier, after the battle of Uhud. But the companion Ibn 'Abbas said later it was as if the people had never heard it until Abu Bakr recited it that day.
And 'Umar said: when I heard it, my legs gave way, I fell to the ground, and I knew he had died.

teach.h: ALLAH IS ALIVE AND DOES NOT DIE.
teach.b: Abu Bakr loved the Prophet as much as anyone alive, and he wept over him first. Then he pointed everyone past the man they loved, to the One who does not die.
Grief and faith, in the same hour, and neither one canceled the other.

how: Muslims love and honor the Prophet deeply while worshiping God alone, and Abu Bakr's words on the day he died are often quoted to explain that distinction; God is called al-Hayy, the Living.

o: the Merciful, a name for God's compassion
the Most High, a name for God above all
the Living, a name of God who never dies

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: you were good in life and in death
as if they'd never heard the verse

s: Abu Bakr spoke to the crowd before seeing the Prophet ﷺ
he went straight into Aisha's room first, kissed him and wept.
the verse Abu Bakr recited was new that day
it had come down years earlier, after Uhud. it was as if they'd never heard it.
'Umar's legs gave way when he heard the verse
he said he fell to the ground and knew the Prophet had died.

games.q: you're Abu Bakr. the Prophet ﷺ has died, 'Umar is telling the crowd he hasn't, and the people are coming apart. what do you do first?
o: argue with 'Umar in front of everyone.
go in to the Prophet, kiss him and weep.
call a council to choose a leader.
games.why: he went in first, uncovered the Prophet's face, kissed him and wept. only then did he go out and speak.

practice: Think of something or someone you've built your days around, a person, a job, a routine, a place, and imagine for a moment it's gone; let yourself feel it, since Abu Bakr wept first. Then ask what's still here underneath.
If you pray, you can say quietly: Allah lives, for Muslims call God al-Hayy, the Living; if you don't, just rest on whatever in you feels steady.

wordCard.voice: Al-Hayy. The Living — one of the names of God, invoked in Abu Bakr's words that Muhammad died but God is alive and does not die. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Living, one of the names of God: alive and never dying.

carryVoice: Your line: allah is alive and does not die. Abu Bakr wept first, and still he said it. That's day two hundred ninety-one.
